newsitem.title: USA: Zenith unveils details of new marketing push.
newsitem.headline: Zenith unveils details of new marketing push.

text.p: Zenith Electronics Corp. is trying to put a bit of the old fire back into its brand image with the next phase of a marketing and brand repositioning campaign featuring a new look, a concert tour promotion and a heavy fall advertising lineup.

The Glenview, Ill.-based company has endured more than a decade of losses. Now, under the leadership of new Chief Executive Peter Willmott, and with support from majority owner LG Electronics Inc. of South Korea, Zenith has set out to update its image as a stodgy-but-good maker of consumer electronics.

Despite a five-year hiatus from national advertising, Zenith is still the 12th-most recognized trademark in the United States, William Sims, president of Zenith Sales Co., the company's domestic sales and marketing division, said in an interview this week.
"We haven't taken advantage of one of the strongest trademarks in U.S. history. It's time we did, and we're going to," Sims added.

Zenith's new logo -- a more upright version of the traditional lightning bolt "Z" -- is intended to signal a new age for a company that to many symbolizes the old guard, rather than the vanguard, of consumer electronics.

With the new look, Zenith hopes to catch the attention of high-wage earners, aged 25 to 49, who are more likely to buy the higher-end and more profitable projection TV and large-screen TV sets in Zenith's line.
Currently, Zenith is most popular with consumers aged 49 and older, who are more inclined to purchase lower-margin, smaller-screen sets.
Robert Gutenstein, an analyst with Kalb Voorhis & Co.in New York, said Zenith's repositioning makes sense at this time.

"The whole thing since Mr. Willmott came on (in November) is to restructure and refocus. Obviously, they're not showing us all the cards, but they're showing a new dynamic that we've only seen in the last six to nine months, which relates to LG (Electronics) and its vision."
Aided by its new advertising agency, Chicago's Bagby & Co., Zenith set out to reach for its higher-end target in February in the first phase of its estimated $10 million to $15 million campaign.
That phase included cable TV buys on Turner Broadcasting outlets and a high-profile ad in Time Warner Inc.'s "Sports Illustrated" swimsuit issue. The company has already seen results.

"The promotions in the first quarter were a dramatic success in the category we want to grow in. We far exceeded industry numbers in the 27-inch direct-view category," Sims said. "We're well on our way to a successful year and future."
Through April, Zenith's sales in direct-view sets 27 inches and larger grew more than 50 percent. In projection TV, growth exceeded 30 percent for the same period, Sims said.
The growth pushed Zenith into the No. 2 position in the market behind RCA, with Magnavox at No. 3, he said.
This summer, Zenith will be the exclusive title sponsor of the 1997 Blues Music Festival national tour, featuring B.B. King and the Robert Cray Band. Beginning in June, the tour will hit 40 cities.

Zenith also plans a consumer sweepstakes and a dealer promotion to generate awareness of Zenith and the tour. Grand prize is an all-expense-paid trip to B.B. King's Memphis Blues Club, and an autographed "Lucille" guitar.

The tour will be followed this fall by an advertising blitz, with Zenith ads appearing on outdoor boards and in fall issues of 30 national magazines, including some unlikely titles for Zenith, such as Playboy, Rolling Stone, GQ and Martha Stewart Living.

The ads take a human approach, focusing on how Zenith products will fit into consumers' lifestyles. Ad copy delivers such messages as, "Choose your own view," "Big fun ... That's the point, isn't it?" and "Big scream TV."
Although Zenith offers strong products and a strong plan for the future, it has at times failed to execute as well as it should have, said Jim Magid, an analyst with Needham & Co.
"If they don't execute well, the promotion and the advertising won't help much," he said. "But, if they do, it will be spectacular."
